title: Field Service total operating model
thesis: Service strategy works only on the diagonal, where business model, operating scenario, and KPIs agree.
howToRead: Find where the client says they are, then where they behave. The gap between the two is the engagement.

rows.summary: The business-model spectrum follows TSIA's research on field services moving from cost center to profit engine to outcome-based offers, and the four supplier levels in B4B. The self-rating statements and conversation guides are adapted from Microsoft Dynamics 365 Field Service sales guidance. The coherence band is RSM analysis.

columns.summary: The four service scenarios come from Gartner's The Future of Field Service Management, which separates them on two factors: control and accountability over equipment outcomes, and service complexity and asset focus. Gartner's Critical Capabilities for Field Service Management then scored vendors against three of them as use cases (appointment-, equipment-, and outcome-centric); knowledge-centric appears in the scenarios only. Gartner retired the Magic Quadrant and Critical Capabilities for this market after 2022 and now publishes a Market Guide.

coherence.label: Aligned
coherence.description: Business model, scenario, and KPIs agree.

coherence.label: Transitional
coherence.description: Moving between models; one of the three lags.

coherence.label: Incoherent
coherence.description: The model and the operation contradict each other.

coherence.label: The trap
coherence.description: Looks aligned on paper; behaves like a cost center.

rows.label: Servitizing
rows.description: Service is sold as a promised outcome rather than as labor and parts.

profile.headline: Servitizing customers care about driving long-term business outcomes.

says.goals: Our whole business has become a service business. We make products, but we sell them as services that drive customer outcomes.
says.success: We're successful when our customers reach their goals, because our business model is built on outcomes.
says.pricing: We sell our products and services on an outcome basis.

challenges: Commoditization that squeezes profit and blurs differentiation
Competitors testing new business models that disrupt the market
Rising customer expectations for new services
Connected equipment (IoT) that demands new capabilities
starters: What is your strategy for differentiating as your products commoditize?
What role do services play in your long-term business strategy?
Do you have a plan to open new revenue streams through service?
Are you developing any product-as-a-service offers?
How are you responding to competitors who are?

rows.label: Profit Center
rows.description: Service is its own margin line with revenue and margin targets.

profile.headline: Profit center customers care about increasing margins.

says.goals: Service keeps our products running, but more importantly it sets us apart from the competition.
says.success: We're successful when outstanding service builds customer loyalty and delivers strong margins.
says.pricing: We sell our services at a fixed price.

items: Finding issues before the customer does
Capturing sales opportunities in the field

challenges: Failures that cannot be anticipated, which raise downtime and frustrate customers
Unprepared technicians, which cut efficiency and satisfaction
No customer history in the field, so preferences are missed
No sales tools in the field, so upsell and cross-sell are lost
Unnecessary visits that erode productivity and margin
starters: What are you doing to stay competitive as products commoditize?
How are you making sure service helps you stand out from competitors?
How often do customers get frustrated because a technician could not fix it the first time?
How often do maintenance issues take more than one visit?
How do you make sure the right people, tools, and parts reach each visit?

rows.label: Cost Center
rows.description: Service exists to protect the product sale and is managed to cost.

profile.headline: Cost center customers care about minimizing expenses.

says.goals: Our service organization exists to support the products we make and repair them when they break.
says.success: We're successful when we service our products effectively while keeping costs down.
says.pricing: We price the service we provide on a cost-plus basis.

challenges: Little visibility into asset performance, so failures are hard to anticipate
Limited diagnostics, so technicians cannot spot the issue before they arrive
Low first-time fix rates, which raise the cost of every job
Technicians, tools, and parts that are not coordinated
Service calls that did not need to happen
starters: How often do technicians need more than one visit to close a request?
What does it cost every time you dispatch a technician to a customer site?
How do you usually learn that equipment is failing?
How often do you send a technician to check equipment that turns out to be working?
How often can a technician not fix the issue because they lack the right parts, tools, or expertise?

columns.label: Appointment-Centric
columns.description: Booked visits to a location, judged on hitting the window.

columns.label: Equipment-Centric
columns.description: Work against a serialized installed asset, judged on fixing it.

columns.label: Knowledge-Centric
columns.description: Resolution depends on expertise, often delivered remotely.

columns.label: Outcome-Centric
columns.description: The customer buys uptime, output, or usage, not the visit.

cells.oneLiner: Scheduled visits run as a cost of serving the customer.
cells.signal: Cost per job, utilization, schedule adherence

cells.oneLiner: Keeping installed equipment running as a warranty or goodwill obligation, managed to cost.
Help desk and remote support run to contain cost per resolution.
Uptime commitments carried as a cost of selling the product, not priced on their own.
Paid, booked visits such as installs and inspections, run for margin.
cells.signal: Claims profit, prices cost-plus, measures efficiency

cells.oneLiner: Service run as a margin line on a contracted installed base.
Expert and remote diagnostic services sold as a margin line.
Priced performance guarantees layered onto a margin-run service business.
Recurring subscription visits where the customer buys the schedule, not the job.
Equipment as a service: the customer pays for the asset's availability.
Subscription access to expertise, monitoring, and remote resolution.
Pay-per-outcome contracts for uptime, output, or usage.
cells.signal: NRR, ARR, SLA attainment, outcome pricing
